title: tailscaled fails to start if tpm state migration fails
body:
### What is the issue?

upgrading from 1.88.4 to 1.90.1 on debian forky, the tailscaled service fails to start when it tries to migrate the state to the tpm.  

this should probably fail open instead of failing closed

noticed this first on a CTL Chromebox CBx2 (board name `wyvern`) which is flashed with https://docs.mrchromebox.tech/ coreboot firmware

note that on another older Chromebox (a Samsung Series 3, board name `stumpy`), this issue doesn't occur, but the state doesn't appear to migrate.  the older devices have more traditional TPMs.

i think this issue will repro on any Chrome OS device which is equipped with Cr50 which is roughly anything late-2017 or newer, and flashed to coreboot


in the logs, see something like 
```
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73922]: getLocalBackend error: store.New: failed to migrate existing state file to TPM-sealed format: newTPMStore("/var/lib/tailscale/tailscaled.state.tmp"): failed to write initial state file: failed to seal state file: failed to seal encryption key to TPM: tpm2.CreatePrimary: TPM_RC_BAD_AUTH (session 1): authorization failure without DA implications
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname systemd[1]: tailscaled.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: logtail started
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: Program starting: v1.90.1-t724a8a253-g726972ec3, Go 1.25.3: []string{"/usr/sbin/tailscaled", "--cleanup"}
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: LogID: 959e98164328a7ee3fc7c2586bccf23959306638bd5a9568f42893cf14d08318
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: logpolicy: using $STATE_DIRECTORY, "/var/lib/tailscale"
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: dns: [resolved-ping=yes rc=resolved resolved=nss nm=yes nm-resolved=yes nm-safe=no resolv-conf-mode=stub ret=systemd-resolved]
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: dns: using "systemd-resolved" mode
Oct 23 12:33:18 systemname tailscaled[73976]: creating dns cleanup: route ip+net: no such network interface
Oct 23 12:33:19 systemname tailscaled[73976]: flushing log.
Oct 23 12:33:19 systemname tailscaled[73976]: logger closing down
Oct 23 12:33:19 systemname systemd[1]: tailscaled.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
Oct 23 12:33:19 systemname systemd[1]: tailscaled.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1.
```


### Steps to reproduce

- flash a chromebox with mrchromebox coreboot firmware
- install debian forky
- install tailscale 1.88.4, works fine
- upgrade to tailscale 1.90.1 via apt, and the service fails to start
- downgrade to 1.88.4 via apt, tailscaled starts again

### Are there any recent changes that introduced the issue?

the auto migration of state to be tpm backed

### OS

Linux

### OS version

debian 14

### Tailscale version

1.90.1

### Other software

_No response_

### Bug report

BUG-959e98164328a7ee3fc7c2586bccf23959306638bd5a9568f42893cf14d08318-20251023174132Z-6d7205ce66aa9665

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: IMO, if Tailscale wants to use TPM it should verify that 2.0 is available before trying to use it. This seems to be due to trying to use 2.0 API features with only 1.2 enabled.

comments.author: participant4

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
For anyone affected, `TS_ENCRYPT_STATE=false` passed to `tailscaled` (for example via `/etc/default/tailscaled`) should fix the crash on startup.

There appear to be a couple of different issues reported here.

1. TPM 1.2 being used as a TPM 2.0 device. This is because on Linux we use `github.com/google/go-tpm/tpm2/transport/linuxtpm.Open` which opens the device file but doesn't actually verify that this is a TPM 2.0 device. This is straightforward to fix by trying to run any command before reporting that a TPM is supported in tailscaled. This should address the erorr that @participant1 and @participant2 see.
2. @participant3, your error is slightly different. Do you have a `/dev/tpm0` on your filesystem? can you run `sudo tpm2_getcap --tcti 'device:/dev/tpm0' properties-fixed`?
3. @reporter your issue appears to be about TPM configuration on the system, it's locked down in some way that I don't fully understand yet. I'll have to read about that chromebox firmware a bit more.

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
@reporter as for chrome OS, this might be the reason: https://<redacted-host>/developers/design-documents/tpm-usage/#tpm-ownership-and-restrictions
I read that as "chrome OS will generate an authorization policy for the Owner hierarchy with a random password and expect the user to write it down" (maybe it's just the login password, not sure). In any case, it looks like there are situations when the Owner hierarchy (where we store the encryption key for the state file) is just not available to tailscaled, so mayhaps we have to probe that at startup and pretend like the TPM is not available.

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
Quick data point - Linux 5.10.103-v7+ boxes running 1.88.4 failed to upgrade to 1.90.1 - 1500km away .. 😢

For a paid service focused on remote access, one might expect the service to roll back on a failed upgrade. I'll take the blame for updating a remote system without a backup interface, but I think there needs to be some reflection on the tailscale side after this issue is resolved. This is a pretty serious gap made apparent by this bug. I can't imagine how many remote units like mine were lost today.

comments.author: participant9
comments.body:
What I see here is not just a bug. What this thread will be a direct result of: The feature they are trying to support is going to be hopelessly lost due to frantic IT admins disabling the TPM feature on their boxes. I did the same, I don't care. The point remains the same, these things happen. I stated the consequence. Is this really an issue??? Probably not. However, if TPM2.0 becomes a requirment because our overlords say it must, I fear all hope is lost. TPM2.0 should remain a feature, not a requirement. What it's capable is nice in theory but just like everything else in this world, hardware based encryption is not and will never be the "one" solution to protect us. We haven't found the real solution and all hardware based encryption will do is slow someone down, not stop them. I'm not trying to incite an arguement so don't freak out, please. I'm just stating a fact from an unbiased person. I neither like nor dislike hardware based encryption. Unformtunately, me, like many others have been forced to use one. (This is where the sour feel comes from). all that said, Please test something this game-changing in the future!!! cheers!

edit... for whatever it matters, I have a plethora of servers, multiple makes and models. The raspberry pi 5 probably has a tpm which is why it stayed online. 9 other boxes went down during the routine mass update I run weekly. I'm not running the update on my remote servers this week because I have not verified they all have tpm 2.0

I'm back online with version 1.88.4 as opposed to 1.90.1 which threw errors on tailscaled startup following the package upgrade. That will mark it for downgrade in Synaptic. comments.body:
I'm glad I'm not the only one who just experienced this same error on my little rinky dink homeserver when I updated Tailscale! I'm running Fedora 42 Server Edition on an old, refurbished laptop that does *not* possess TPM 2 capabilities. I was really confused when `tailscaled` failed to initialize and start correctly and broke DNS resolution for me; I have my DNS sinkhole setup and configured through this machine, so that wasn't pleasant to see websites not loading on my other devices.

Directly running `tailscaled` gave me this last output:
```plaintext
getLocalBackend error: store.New: failed to migrate existing state file to TPM-sealed format: newTPMStore("/var/lib/tailscale/tailscaled.state.tmp"): failed to write initial state file: failed to seal state file: failed to seal encryption key to TPM: tpm2.CreatePrimary: unrecognized error code (0x1e)
```
This seems to line up with everyone else has already discussed about TPM 2 issues. And I saw someone here also mentioned they are using a T400 series Thinkpad. A simple downgrade doing `sudo dnf downgrade tailscale` rolled my package back to `1.88.4`.

I love the Tailscale team, but please pay a little mind about older or stranger hardware configuration that exists out there. 😅

However, I understand this is necessary to protect the amount of state that has to been stored for tailnet stuff based on the threat model.

Though, I am curious. If encryption of the state is achieved using TPM2-related capabilities, what is the option for protecting the state for hardware that isn't TPM2-ready? Is the only option to not have the state encrypted because of the threat model? I recall that in [Tailscale: Encrypting Data At Rest](https://tailscale.com/blog/encrypting-data-at-rest) that Tailscale is designed to use the TPM as a means of performing encryption (in regards to the key material) with protection from a potentially compromised userspace?

comments.author: participant5
comments.body:
Sorry for the breakage everyone. The fix is merged and we should release 1.90.2 today.

To clarify some potential confusion about this feature: TPM 2.0 is not going to be a requirement for using Tailscale, this is not another Windows 11 situation.

The feature requires a TPM 2.0 device on Windows and Linux to work (it uses other means on macOS/iOS/Android). We had the feature available as opt-in (using `--encrypt-state`) in the last two releases, since 1.86. The change in 1.90 is to automatically enable the feature **only if a TPM 2.0 device is available on the host**. I botched that check - the code only ensured that `/dev/tpmrm0` or `/dev/tpm0` is present and accessible, but it also exists for TPM 1.2 devices. A secondary problem is that on some devices with TPM 2.0, the TPM is configured with an extra authorization requirement making it not usable by Tailscale.
The fix in 1.90.2 will account for those situations.

> Though, I am curious. If encryption of the state is achieved using TPM2-related capabilities, what is the option for protecting the state for hardware that isn't TPM2-ready? Is the only option to not have the state encrypted because of the threat model?

@participant12 correct. We haven't found a way to safely encrypt the state file without something like a TPM on Linux and Windows. We could encrypt and toss the encryption keys somewhere else on disk, but that's just security through obscurity and not a real mitigation.

comments.body:
1.90.2 for Linux is now published. Please report here if you still have issues with tailscaled startup.

@participant10 there was some debate internally about pulling the release but now it's too late as the fix is published :)

As for metrics - if tailscaled crashes at startup after an upgrade, that looks no different from our control plane perspective than a machine just going to sleep or Tailscale being deleted on it. We don't even know that a node is updated until it reconnects and reports a newer version.
In the last 2 days there was no noticeable change in the total number of connected nodes. I know that a number of users reported the problem here, but very few people (relative to the total user count) actually update to the latest version as soon as it's available.

For this particular issue we will try to at least test in CI to catch regressions: https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/17626

The new version is indeed fixed, starts correctly with a benign `failed to create hardware attestation key: tpm2.CreatePrimary: unrecognized error code (0xa)`

> As for metrics - if tailscaled crashes at startup after an upgrade, that looks no different from our control plane perspective than a machine just going to sleep or Tailscale being deleted on it. We don't even know that a node is updated until it reconnects and reports a newer version.

I was guessing this was the case. With some data crunching, you could identify nodes that appear to have auto-update enabled (evidenced by upgrading between versions multiple times over a time period) and track these specifically as their becoming offline after new release has more information value. Even if in bulk total node count doesn't go down, the ones that do auto-update would be especially valuable to catch issues early. Kind of like an organic canary.

No matter I restart the `tailscaled.service` or reboot the machine, it now works fine.

* With previous 1.90.x versions, `tailscaled.service` failed to start (Last working version was 1.88.4)
* This issue only happens on one of my Debian 13 x64 host - My other x64 or arm devices (Debian 13 and Windows 11) don't show this issue with v1.90.x
* Previous workaround from some comments (`TS_ENCRYPT_STATE=false, FLAGS="--encrypt-state=false"`) didn't help on this problematic Debian 13 host - And I don't have this workaround with the latest working v1.92.1.
* Even on this problematic Debian host, which has native dual systems with Win 11 (not on virtual machine), if I switch to Win 11, this issue was not found with v1.90.x (so it should not be pure hardware problem)
